lessons.title: Components, Props, and Composition
lessons.summary: A component is a function that describes UI for current inputs.
lessons.body:
Components, Props, and Composition

Why this matters
A component is a function that describes UI for current inputs. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• A component is a function that describes UI for current inputs.
• Props flow from parent to child; children/composition let parents supply structure without creating giant configurable components.
• Keep rendering pure: the same inputs should describe the same output.
• Split components by responsibility and reuse, not every HTML element.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, react foundations i stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter components, props, and composition again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.title: Events and Local State
lessons.summary: Event handlers respond to user actions and are appropriate places to start mutations or update interaction state.
lessons.body:
Events and Local State

Why this matters
Event handlers respond to user actions and are appropriate places to start mutations or update interaction state. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Event handlers respond to user actions and are appropriate places to start mutations or update interaction state.
• useState stores values that must persist between renders and whose changes should re-render UI.
• State updates are scheduled; do not assume setting state changes the current render's variable immediately.
• Use functional updates when next state depends on previous state.

lessons.title: Derived Values and Single Source of Truth
lessons.summary: If a value can be computed from props/state during render, usually derive it instead of storing a synchronized copy.
lessons.body:
Derived Values and Single Source of Truth

Why this matters
If a value can be computed from props/state during render, usually derive it instead of storing a synchronized copy. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• If a value can be computed from props/state during render, usually derive it instead of storing a synchronized copy.
• Duplicate state creates synchronization paths and stale bugs.
• Lift state to the nearest common owner only when multiple children need coordinated access.
• Later, server data belongs in a server-state tool rather than copied into local state.

lessons.title: Lists, Keys, and Identity
lessons.summary: Keys tell React which list item identity persists across reordering/insertion/deletion.
lessons.body:
Lists, Keys, and Identity

Why this matters
Keys tell React which list item identity persists across reordering/insertion/deletion. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Keys tell React which list item identity persists across reordering/insertion/deletion.
• Use stable domain IDs rather than array indexes when item order can change.
• A key is not passed as a normal prop automatically.
• Identity mistakes can make input state appear to jump between rows.

lessons.title: Basic Form Handling Before Libraries
lessons.summary: Controlled inputs use React state as the displayed value; uncontrolled inputs let DOM hold current value and can be read through form APIs/refs.
lessons.body:
Basic Form Handling Before Libraries

Why this matters
Controlled inputs use React state as the displayed value; uncontrolled inputs let DOM hold current value and can be read through form APIs/refs. This lesson is intentionally framework-light. You are building a mental model that will be reused when Next.js, NestJS, Prisma, TanStack Query, and deployment tooling add more vocabulary. The goal is not to memorize definitions. The goal is to predict what the computer will do and know where to look when reality differs from that prediction.

Mental model
• Controlled inputs use React state as the displayed value; uncontrolled inputs let DOM hold current value and can be read through form APIs/refs.
• Prevent default submission only when handling the request in JavaScript.
• Labels, names, autocomplete, input types, and native constraints still matter in React.
• Form libraries later optimize boilerplate but do not change the underlying browser semantics.

Step-by-step walkthrough
1. Write the concept in your own words before using a tool. If your explanation depends on framework jargon, simplify it one level.
2. Create the smallest runnable example that demonstrates only this concept. Keep it outside the main TaskFlow repository if experimentation could create noise.
3. Predict the result before running the command or clicking the UI. Prediction makes the output evidence instead of entertainment.
4. Run it and capture what actually happened: terminal output, browser state, request details, or file changes.
5. Change one assumption and repeat. Try an invalid input, wrong path, missing field, reordered data, or other safe failure relevant to the topic.
6. Explain the difference between the successful and failing runs. That explanation is the transferable skill.

TaskFlow connection
Later in the course, react foundations i stops being an isolated topic and becomes infrastructure for real features. When you encounter basic form handling before libraries again, ask which layer owns it, what its inputs are, what output proves success, and what failure evidence is available. That prevents you from copying framework snippets without understanding the underlying browser, runtime, operating-system, or language behavior.

Guided exercise
Create a tiny example from scratch without copying the final code from a tutorial. Keep the example under about 30–50 lines where possible. After it works, deliberately break one assumption. Write the exact symptom and the smallest fix. Then delete the experiment or commit it in a dedicated practice folder so it does not pollute production project structure.

Check your understanding
• Can you describe the concept without naming a framework?
• Can you point to the exact input and output?
• Can you name one common incorrect assumption?
• Can you reproduce the idea in a tiny example?
• Can you diagnose one intentional failure using evidence rather than guesses?

Instructor note
Do not rush because the syntax looks easy. Most difficult full-stack bugs are not caused by forgetting syntax; they come from an incorrect model of ownership, execution environment, identity, time, or data flow. The foundation track exists so later lessons can move quickly without becoming mysterious.

lessons.body:
Lab: Basic Form Handling Before Libraries

Purpose
This lab converts the previous explanation into a small piece of evidence you created yourself. Do not begin by copying the finished example. Start with the behavior you expect, then make the computer prove or disprove your model.

Your task
Build the smallest runnable example for “Basic Form Handling Before Libraries”, predict its output, change one assumption, and explain the difference using concrete evidence.

Working method
1. Create the smallest clean starting point.
2. Predict the first result in writing.
3. Implement only enough to test that prediction.
4. Run it and capture the result.
5. Add one intentional failure or changed assumption.
6. Diagnose from evidence before editing randomly.
7. Restore the correct behavior.
8. Close the reference and reproduce the important part from memory.

Why this is separate from the concept lesson
Reading can create familiarity without recall. The separate lab forces retrieval, execution, and debugging. Those three abilities are what later framework lessons assume when the codebase becomes larger.

Definition of done
You have a runnable example, one recorded prediction, one successful result, one controlled failure with diagnosis, and a short explain-back in your own words.
